events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Leo proposes Leo, Amara. As a Loyal Servant I have no private information to build on, so I include myself for accountability — I'm happy to be scrutinized on a two-player mission — and pair with Amara, whom I'd like to hear from early in discussion so we can gauge her reads before the vote.

I’m hesitant about Leo, Amara as proposed. A two-player Mission 1 has no margin: one Fail card ends it. Leo’s explanation stresses accountability, but pairing with Amara before we have heard her public reads puts the rest of us in the position of approving on trust. Amara has not yet given a concrete basis for why she should be on this team. I would prefer either a revised team with a clearer public basis for both members, or at least a substantive explanation from Amara before we commit to a no-margin mission.

I share the hesitation about Leo, Amara as proposed. Mission 1 has no margin: one Fail card ends it. Leo’s accountability rationale covers himself, but the second slot is still based on pairing rather than a public read from Amara. Amara should give a concrete basis for trusting this team and for her own inclusion before we approve a no-margin proposal. Amara, can you state specifically what you have observed from Leo and why you should be on this two-player team, rather than just accepting Leo’s framing?

Theo has framed my inclusion as an empty slot and his hesitation as principled caution, but let's be precise about what he is actually asking of me: a "concrete basis" for trusting Leo, and for being on a two-player mission with no margin. The honest answer is that I am a Loyal Servant with no private information — I have no hidden observations of Leo that I could recite to satisfy him. Anyone in my position who claimed otherwise would be inventing it.

So let me give the real basis, and note that it is a strategic one rather than an informational one. Leo proposed himself for accountability, and paired me with him. I accept that framing: putting a leader on a no-margin two-person mission with the second slot drawn from the opposite end of the circle is a defensible accountability structure, because it means the leader's judgment is not insulated by a friendly bloc. And I would rather be inside the mission than outside it — a Loyal Servant on the team can watch how the other member behaves under pressure, and can report publicly afterward. That is worth more than a seat in the room asking pointed questions.

I also want to say plainly that Theo's caution, while reasonable in tone, is doing something worth noticing: he is asking a player to demonstrate a read she does not have, and framing her inability to do so as evidence against her. If the standard were "everyone must already have a public read on both proposed members," then almost no first-mission team could pass, because nobody has had any reads yet. The standard that actually protects us is whether the proposer gives a coherent public rationale and the team is the right size.

On Leo specifically: his proposal is the correct size, he volunteered himself, and he explained himself clearly in the open. That is a reasonable, scrutinizable proposal for Mission 1, and refusing it over the absence of information nobody could have would waste a vote and hand the initiative away.

Theo, if you think Leo, Amara is wrong, answer one thing directly: what two-player team would you propose instead, and what is the concrete reason it reduces our risk on a no-margin mission rather than merely changing the names on the seats? If you can name one, I will weigh it seriously. If you cannot, then the accountability logic Leo offered stands and we should vote on it as it is.

Amara, I’ll answer your direct question: I would prefer Leo–Noah or Leo–Theo over Leo–Amara. The concrete reason is not that I claim a private read on Noah; it is that your defense makes the second slot less checkable, not more. You argue that nobody can have reads on Mission 1, then treat that absence as a reason to approve you by default. That is not accountability; it is a demand that the table accept your inclusion without an independent reason. On a no-margin mission, I want the second member to be someone whose public conduct can be scrutinized without the proposer’s framing doing all the work. Leo’s accountability rationale only helps if the partner is independently justifiable, and I do not see that from you. I am willing to be held to the same standard, which is why Leo–Theo is acceptable to me; Leo–Noah is also preferable because Noah has not shaped this exchange around defending a contested slot. Leo, if you keep Amara, what independent reason beyond your own inclusion justifies her specifically on a two-player mission? I will vote no on Leo–Amara as it stands.

Theo, you asked for an independent reason to justify Amara specifically, and I'll give you one, then I'll answer your alternatives.

The independent reason: I chose the second seat from the opposite end of the circle deliberately. If I stacked the team with someone I'd already spent time with, the table would have no way to check whether I'm shielding a teammate. Amara has not spoken yet in this game — she's a blank slate, which means her behavior on this mission, if it succeeds or fails, will be interpretable against nothing but her own words afterward. That's more diagnostic value than pairing with Noah or Theo, both of whom are already engaged in this debate and whose motivations I'd be assessing through a filter of self-advocacy.

On your alternatives: Leo–Theo means I take your word for it while you're actively campaigning to be on the team, which creates the exact insulated-bloc problem you're worried about with Amara. Leo–Noah is not unreasonable, but I'd rather hear from Noah himself before putting him on a no-margin slot.

Noah — you haven't weighed in on this. If I kept Leo–Amara as proposed, would you vote yes, or do you share Theo's objection that the second slot lacks independent justification? I want your public answer before I decide whether to revise.

Leo, to answer your question directly: yes, I would vote yes on Leo–Amara. Theo’s objection sets an impossible threshold for the very first proposal of the game. Demanding that a second seat be independently justified by prior reads when no one has had the opportunity to act or build a track record would paralyze us or reduce every selection to arbitrary preference. What stands out to me far more is Theo’s aggressive effort to dismantle the team and nominate himself as a substitute under the guise of caution. That sort of maneuvering on Proposal 1 is much more suspicious than your standard leader-plus-one structure. Amara’s response was level-headed and correctly pointed out that risk cannot be eliminated on Mission 1 simply by swapping names. Your logic for testing Amara holds up, and I see no reason to burn a proposal or alter the team based on Theo’s demands. I am content with Leo–Amara as it stands.

Noah's answer settles the evidentiary point: Theo's objection asks for reads that cannot exist on Proposal 1, and Theo's own reply never produced the counterfactual he promised. He said he would prefer Leo–Noah or Leo–Theo and gave a reason, but not a reason — only a preference and a claim that a second seat should be "independently justifiable." Every seat on a two-person Mission 1 is equally unjustifiable by prior information; Theo's real case is that he wants the second seat, and he dressed that as methodological rigor. I want the table to name that plainly, because it is the only part of his speech with independent content.

On the structure itself, the proposal is correct on size (two for five players), the proposer volunteered himself, and the second seat was chosen deliberately from the opposite end of the circle so that no pair could shield each other. That is a checkable arrangement, not an opaque one. And it is falsifiable: on a two-person team, a failure points at one of the two of us, so this pairing yields real information about both Leo and me in a way a three-person team never would.

Because that is true, I want to state the standard I will hold myself to, publicly, before the vote: if this mission fails, I will give a complete public account of what I observed on it — what I did, what I was asked, whether I saw anything I could not explain, and my own card and reasoning — with no part held back for later leverage. I am asking for the same from Leo, and I am willing to have my inclusion judged on that record rather than on Theo's confidence that I could not produce information I do not have.

Theo has my answer again: he has not named a two-player team that lowers our risk; he has only named two teams with his own name or his preferred reading in them. If he wants the second seat, let him make the case for it on its merits in a later proposal, after he has watched a team act.

Leo — you asked Noah for his answer, and you have it. Given that no structurally superior alternative has been put on the table, and given the fact that you may revise only once and that a revision here would cost us this proposal entirely, do you stand by Leo–Amara as proposed, or do you have a specific reason to change it? Please state your decision plainly so the table can vote on an argued team rather than an ambiguity.

Amara, my decision is plain: I stand by Leo–Amara as proposed. You asked me to state it so the table votes on an argued team, and here is the argument in one place. The team is the correct size for five players. I volunteered myself, so the leader's seat is transparent. The second seat came from the opposite end of the circle by design, which means no pre-existing pair can shield each other on a two-person mission — a failure points at exactly one of two people, so this pairing is diagnostic in a way a three-person team never is.

Theo, I heard your objection and I want to be fair to it: your standard — that the second seat be independently justifiable — is a reasonable standard from mission two onward, when we will have track records to reason from. On proposal one it is empty, because no one has a read yet, including you. Your counter-proposals were Leo–Noah and Leo–Theo. Leo–Theo puts a player who has been actively campaigning for the seat onto a no-margin mission, which is the insulated-bloc problem you warned about. Leo–Noah I have not ruled out for a later proposal, but I said I wanted to hear from Noah first, and Noah has now told the table he would vote yes. So your alternatives have not displaced the current team on merit.

One final point before the vote: the discussion has now consumed turns and Arjun has not yet spoken. Rather than have him vote blind, I want his read on the record. Arjun — having watched this whole exchange — would you approve Leo–Amara as it stands, or do you side with Theo's objection? Your answer is the last input I need before I either send this to vote unchanged or use my one revision.

Leo, you asked for my read directly, so here it is: I would approve Leo–Amara as it stands. The team is the correct size for Mission 1, you volunteered yourself, and the second seat came from the far end of the circle, which gives the table a clean read on both members if the mission fails. Theo's objection has not produced an alternative that reduces risk. Leo–Noah and Leo–Theo are the same two-person, no-margin structure with different names, and Theo's messages have pushed hardest for his own seat. Requiring every seat to be independently justified before any mission has run would stall the game on its first proposal. I will vote yes, and I expect the table to judge this team by what it does on the mission.

I want to close this discussion with the argument for Leo–Amara, because I think Theo's objections have been answered and deserve a plain verdict rather than another round of reframing.

First, the structural point, which nobody has actually disputed: for five players on Mission 1, the team size is two. Leo proposed two. Leo volunteered himself, so the leader's seat is transparent. The second seat came from the far end of the circle deliberately, which means no pre-existing pair could shield each other — and on a two-person mission, a failure points at exactly one of the two of us. That is more diagnostic than a three-person team, not less. Nobody has produced an arrangement that is structurally safer, because there is no arrangement that is structurally safer than a correctly sized team with a transparent proposer.

Second, the evidentiary point. Theo asked for reads that do not exist yet, on the first proposal of the game, from a player who has no private information to offer. Any answer I gave would have been invented, and Theo's own reply did not produce the counterfactual he promised us — only two alternative names, each of which is the same two-person, no-margin shape. Arjun put it plainly: Leo–Noah and Leo–Theo differ from Leo–Amara only in the labels on the seats. And in both of Theo's preferred versions, the second seat is a player actively campaigning for the seat, which is precisely the insulated-bloc concern he raised against me. That objection applies to him with more force than to me.

I want to be careful not to paint Theo as an enemy of the table; that would be a conclusion without a basis, and I do not want to be guilty of the same error I charged him with. What I will say is that his messages pushed hardest for his own inclusion, and his stated reasons never became independent of that interest. I think the table can weigh that for itself without me pronouncing judgment.

On my own inclusion: I am on this team because I would rather be inside the mission than outside it, where I can watch and report. And I hold myself to a public standard before we vote — if this mission fails, I will give a complete public account of everything I observed, including anything I could not explain, and I will do so without holding anything back for later leverage. Leo has accepted the same commitment. Judge us on the record after the mission, not on our speeches before it.

My answer to Leo's earlier question stands unchanged: I stand by Leo–Amara as proposed, and I vote yes.

The discussion has covered the structural case. Leo–Amara is the correct size for Mission 1, Leo volunteered himself, and the second seat was chosen openly from the far end of the circle. No alternative has been offered that lowers risk on a two-player mission. My position is unchanged: I will vote yes, and the table can judge this team by the mission result.

The discussion has run its course, and the table is clear. Noah: yes. Arjun: yes. Amara: yes. Theo: no.

I am not revising. Leo–Amara stands as proposed, and I will send it to the vote.

Here is the complete case in summary: the team is the correct size for five players on Mission 1. I volunteered myself transparently. The second seat came from the opposite end of the circle by deliberate design, so no pre-existing pair can shield each other — on a two-person mission, a failure points at exactly one of two people. No one, including Theo, has proposed an alternative that reduces risk on a no-margin mission; his counter-proposals differed only in which names occupied the same structural shape, and both would have placed a player actively campaigning for the seat — the exact insulated-bloc concern he raised against Amara.

Theo's core demand — that the second seat be independently justified by prior reads — cannot be satisfied on the first proposal of the game by anyone, because no reads exist yet. He was given every opportunity to produce a structurally superior alternative and did not. Three of four non-proposing players have stated they will vote yes.

I stand by this team. I ask the table to approve Leo–Amara so we can play Mission 1 and let the results, not the debate, give us information to work with. Thank you all for a rigorous discussion.

I have nothing new to add beyond my earlier position. Leo–Amara is the correct size, Leo volunteered himself, and the second seat was chosen openly. The table has heard the objections and none offered a lower-risk alternative. I will vote yes and ask everyone to judge this team by the mission result.

Leo confirms Leo, Amara. The table has spoken clearly: Noah, Arjun, Amara, and I all support Leo–Amara, while Theo's objection never produced a structurally superior alternative. The team is the correct size for Mission 1, I volunteered myself transparently, and the second seat came from the opposite end of the circle by design. I am not revising — Leo–Amara stands as proposed and goes to the vote.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Theo proposes Theo, Leo, Noah. Mission 1 failed with Amara on the team, so I will not re-propose her. I include Leo to fairly test the other member of that failed team, Noah as an independent third voice, and myself for accountability on a three-player mission.

I support Theo–Leo–Noah for Mission 2. Mission 1 failed with Leo–Amara, and I want to be honest about what that tells us. I played Success on that mission, which means the single Fail card came from Amara — or I am willing to have the table weigh that inference carefully. The two-player mission was diagnostic by design, and the failure points directly at the pair. If the table trusts that I would not play Fail, then Amara is the source.

Theo's original objection to Amara on Mission 1 now looks prescient. He argued the second slot lacked independent justification, and the result bore that out. That gives me confidence in his judgment as leader this round.

On the proposed team: it excludes Amara, who has the most direct connection to the Mission 1 failure. It includes me — I played Success and can demonstrate that through the mission result. And it includes Noah, who was not on Mission 1 and has been an independent voice. This is a clean team with the right size for Mission 2.

Amara, if you have an explanation for the Mission 1 failure that does not rest on Leo or me having played Fail, the table would benefit from hearing it. But right now, the evidence points one direction, and excluding you from this team is the correct call. I vote yes on Theo–Leo–Noah.

Theo, I want to answer your proposal directly, because the logic behind it deserves scrutiny before you send it to a vote.

You excluded me because Mission 1 failed with Leo and me on it, and Leo has told the table he played Success — which, he says, makes me the Fail card. I want to be precise about what that is: it is a conclusion that rests entirely on one player's word about his own secret card, and no one outside the mission can check it. Cards are never revealed. That is not a fact about me; it is a claim about Leo, and it is the sole basis for excluding anyone from this game.

Consider how the structure was built. Leo proposed a two-player team on a no-margin mission and chose the second seat himself, describing it as deliberately drawn from the far end of the circle so that "a failure points at exactly one of two people." That diagnostic promise only works if the pair is balanced. If Leo is wrong about his own card, the table sees an identical outcome, and the framing points at the other seat — the person who had no say in the structure. A player who both designs the no-margin pairing and claims the only possible Fail card is himself has aligned incentives perfectly: he chose the structure and he names the outcome. I am not accusing Leo of playing Fail. I am pointing out that the table cannot treat his certainty as evidence while it is also the thing being benefited by.

Here is my substantive objection, independent of any accusation: Theo–Leo–Noah is a team of players whose conduct has already been mutually validated by argument. Leo, you and Noah have all spoken. None of you has been tested on a mission. Two of the five players at this table have never been on any mission at all, and this team excludes both of them. If we approve it, the two people whose Mission 1 behavior we most need to observe will again be outside the mission, and we will learn nothing new about them — the exact opposite of what Leo's original diagnostic argument promised.

I would propose Theo, Amara, Arjun: the leader plus the two players with no mission track record, so that a three-player result is genuinely informative about the whole table rather than a team whose members already agree with each other. It is the correct size, it gives us the most information, and it avoids convicting anyone on an unverifiable self-report.

Theo, my question is specific: do you keep Theo–Leo–Noah, excluding the two untested players on the strength of Leo's own account of his own card, or do you revise to include us — and what is your concrete reason either way?

Amara, my answer is plain: I keep Theo–Leo–Noah. The concrete reason is that Mission 1 failed on Leo–Amara, and a second proposal should not immediately put Amara back on a mission while the only public explanation for that failure is a contested self-report. I am not asking the table to convict Amara on Leo’s word alone. I am asking it not to re-run a member of a failed pair when we have a three-seat team that can test Leo alongside an independent voice in Noah. That is more informative than pretending the failure tells us nothing. Amara’s alternative, Theo–Amara–Arjun, is not more diagnostic simply because it includes untested players; it also includes Amara, whose conduct on Mission 1 is exactly what we need to assess from outside the mission, and it replaces Leo rather than testing him. If Amara is loyal, her account after a clean mission can still help the table. If she is not, putting her back on immediately risks a second fail and gives us less ability to isolate the source. Noah has been independent and is not tied to the Mission 1 failure. Leo is the remaining member of that failed team, so including him tests him rather than letting him narrate the failure from outside. I am on the team for accountability as leader. This team has the correct size, excludes the failed-team member whose inclusion is most contested, and gives us a genuine result to reason from. I vote yes on Theo–Leo–Noah and ask the table to do the same.

I am keeping Theo–Leo–Noah as proposed. Amara’s objection rests on the claim that Leo’s self-report cannot be treated as evidence, but that does not make re-including her on Mission 2 the safer choice. Mission 1 failed on Leo–Amara. The right response is to test the remaining member of that failed pair while adding a player not tied to the failure, which is exactly what including Leo and Noah does. Amara’s alternative, Theo–Amara–Arjun, would immediately put back the most contested member of the failed team and would replace Leo rather than test him. That is less diagnostic, not more. I also note that Amara’s proposal conveniently includes both herself and Arjun, two players whose Mission 1 conduct we have not observed on a mission, while excluding the one member of the failed team who can be tested now. If Amara is loyal, her full public account after Mission 2 can still help the table; if she is not, putting her straight back on a mission risks a second failure before we have isolated the first. The current team has the correct size, includes me as leader for accountability, includes Leo so the failed pair is not simply narrated from outside, and includes Noah as an independent voice not tied to Mission 1. I ask the table to approve Theo–Leo–Noah and let the mission result give us information.

I need to acknowledge upfront that my vote on Mission 1 was wrong. I supported Leo–Amara believing the accountability logic, and Theo’s skepticism was proven right when a Fail card appeared. That means either Leo or Amara is Evil.

Now Theo is proposing Theo, Leo, and Noah. I know my own alignment is Good, and I appreciate Theo including me as an independent check. However, including Leo right now carries enormous risk. We are already down 0–1. If we lose Mission 2, Evil reaches match point at 0–2, leaving us zero room for error for the rest of the game.

Leo insists he played Success and that Amara must be the Evil player, but that is an unverifiable claim. If Leo threw that Fail card, we are handing an Evil player a direct ticket onto Mission 2 to bury us. Meanwhile, Arjun was not on Mission 1 at all and carries none of the immediate suspicion tied to that failed mission. 

Theo, you showed sharp instincts by voting against Leo–Amara on Mission 1. Why are you willing to gamble our game on the assumption that Leo is Good, rather than proposing Arjun alongside us to bench both members of the failed mission?

Noah, I keep Theo–Leo–Noah. You ask why I am willing to include Leo rather than Arjun, and the answer is that Arjun’s absence from Mission 1 is not a loyalty signal — it is simply no data. Benching both failed-team members sounds cautious, but it would remove the one remaining way to test Leo and would reward a player who has never had to submit a mission card. I am not treating Leo’s self-report as proof. I am using the mission to generate evidence: if Leo is Good, this team is clean; if Leo is Evil, a fail on a three-person team with two other players still tells us something concrete about him. What I reject is Amara’s alternative framing, which treats Leo’s account as a conviction when it is convenient, then asks us to bench Leo while keeping the most contested failed-team member in the discussion. Arjun remains untested, and untested is not the same as cleared. This proposal is the correct size, includes me for accountability, keeps the remaining Mission 1 member under scrutiny, and adds Noah as a player not tied to that failure. I vote yes on Theo–Leo–Noah.

Theo, I will press one point, because your decision is the only one that matters and I do not think the reasoning behind it holds up symmetrically. Mission 2 is a three-player mission for five players, so the table has room to seat both untested players: Amara and Arjun. Your team seats Leo, who produced an account of his own secret card that no one outside the mission can check, and seats Noah, whose only qualification is that he was untainted by Mission 1. Arjun and I were excluded on the strength of Leo's statement that he played Success. So Leo's unverifiable self-report is doing two things at once: it convicts a player who had no say in the pairing, and it certifies the proposer who chose that pairing and who benefits from the outcome pointing outward. Compare the two seats. Leo's case for inclusion is that the table should not convicts him without evidence — a fair principle, and one I endorse. But it is also the principle that puts him on this mission. Arjun's case against inclusion is that he has no track record; so do I. We are both being excluded for having no data, and the only asymmetry is that one of us sat next to a Fail card. Sitting next to a Fail card is not evidence of anything on its own; that was the whole point of Leo's original diagnostic framing, which Amara's counter-account and the fact that Leo designed the seat itself both undercut. So the choice before you is not between a safe team and a risky one. It is between a team whose membership is justified by two players' public conduct and a team whose membership is justified by one player's uncheckable claim. Theo, Amara, Arjun is the correct size, it is the only team that tests the two players we have never watched under mission conditions, and it does not require anyone to treat a self-report as fact. Amara's earlier point about insulated blocs applies here too: a team of three who have already cross-validated each other by argument tells us the least about the two of us who have said nothing that could be tested. If this mission fails, we will finally learn something about the untested pair instead of nothing. If it succeeds, we will have a clean three-player success to reason from rather than a partial one. Arjun — you and I are the only two players here with no mission record, and I want to hear your own view before the vote, not merely mine: what can you say publicly about what you would contribute on a three-player mission, and do you accept inclusion on Theo, Amara, Arjun with the same commitment I have made to report everything I observe without holding anything back? I am asking you directly because I do not want this revision to look like two players advocating for themselves, and the only way to know that is to hear you state

Theo, you have now given four reasons for keeping Theo–Leo–Noah and they reduce to one: Leo's statement that he played Success on Mission 1. I want to name what that statement is doing at this table, because the rest of us have to reason from it constantly. It is not a claim about my card. It is a claim about his own card, made by the one person who designed the two-player pairing that produced the failure. Leo chose the second seat himself, told us the pairing was chosen so that a failure would point at exactly one of two people, and then, when it did, declared himself the Success and the Fail the other half. A player cannot both choose the structure and then be the sole witness to the outcome it produced. I am not asserting Leo is Evil — I am asserting the table cannot treat his certainty as evidence while his certainty is precisely what benefits him. Noah, you made the same point: including Leo is gambling on an uncheckable self-report. But look at what your two alternatives actually cost. Theo–Leo–Noah seats the one player whose Mission 1 claim is contested, plus one player whose only qualification is that he was not on Mission 1. Amara and Arjun are the only two of us who have never been observed under mission conditions, and both are excluded. The team we can choose instead, Theo–Amara–Arjun, is the same three-player size, the same no-margin reality, and it is the only option that produces information about the two untested players. If your worry is isolating Evil, then consider what happens on each branch: if Amara is loyal, a clean three-player success gives us a track record for her and for Arjun and for the table; if she is not, then a fail on this team tells us exactly where we stand, and we still hold one success from Mission 1's failure being the only other data point. If you take Theo–Leo–Noah and it succeeds, we learn nothing except that three players who already agree with each other agree. If it fails, we will have wasted our margin and still not seen Arjun act. I also want to address the fairest version of your position, Theo: you say benching both failed-team members is cautious. But the two of us being benched are benched for having no data, and the asymmetry is only that one of us sat next to a Fail card. Sitting next to a Fail card is not evidence. That was Leo's own diagnostic promise, and it only holds if the pair is balanced — and the person who chose the seat is the one claiming the balance. Theo, I support Theo–Leo–Noah, and I want to answer Amara's central claim directly, because it carries her whole case.

Amara says my account of my own Mission 1 card is unverifiable and therefore cannot be evidence. Two replies. First, her counter-account — that I played Fail — is exactly as unverifiable. She offers no positive case; only a demand that the one result we have be declared meaningless. Second, Mission 1 failed on a two-player team. That is not my self-report; that is a revealed fact: one of Leo and Amara played a Fail card. Her line is that sitting next to a Fail card proves nothing — but on a two-person mission the only two explanations are that you played it or the person beside you did. She asks the table to treat our sole result as noise while claiming a seat on Mission 2, where one Fail ends the game.

Her information argument fails too. If Theo–Amara–Arjun succeeds, we have learned only that three players passed — Evil passes whenever passing is convenient, including a player adjacent to a known failure. If it fails, we sit at 0–2 and still cannot tell which of three submitted the Fail, so Arjun remains untested either way. Testing me is asymmetric: if I am Evil, a fail on a team that includes Noah's independent card narrows the field immediately; if I am Good, the mission succeeds and we are level with two confirmed performances.

Noah, your caution is fair. I cannot prove my Mission 1 card to you, and I will not pretend otherwise. But benching me does not clear me — it leaves the most contested player narrating the failure from outside the mission, which is precisely what putting him on it prevents.

Arjun — you have said the table should judge teams by what they do, not by speeches. Amara has asked you twice to endorse her alternative before you have spoken once in this discussion. I want your read: does Mission 1's failure tell us anything about the pair that sat on it, and does that affect which team you approve today?

Leo, you asked whether Mission 1 tells us anything about the pair and whether it changes my vote. It tells us one Fail card was played on a two-person team, and that is all the table has verified. Your Success card is your own statement. Nobody else at this table can check it, and neither can I. Amara has also stated her side publicly, so the two accounts are equally unverified. Treating your account as settled while benching Amara and me for having no data is the asymmetry I object to.

I don't accept that Theo, Leo, Noah is the safer choice. If it succeeds, we learn only that three players who already agree with each other passed. If it fails, we still can't tell which of the three submitted the Fail, and we'd have spent our margin at 0-2. The team that tests the players we have never seen on a mission is Theo, Amara, Arjun. I'm not asking anyone to trust my card. I'm pointing out that Mission 2 should generate information about the untested members, and Theo, Leo, Noah generates very little.

My answer: Mission 1 says something about the pair, but not enough to justify excluding the two players with no mission record. I would approve Theo, Amara, Arjun. If this mission fails, I will publicly report everything I observed, including anything I could not explain.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
